SECTION II Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation by the Faculty Senate ORGANIZATIONAL CHANGES: COLLEGE OF ARTS AND SCIENCES: Africana Studies Program: See Appendix A To make Africana Studies an academic department rather than a program.
Africana Studies has been a program at the University of Rhode Island for more than three decades.
During that time, Africana Studies (referred to as AAF) has always embodied the values of racial and social justice.
AAF has served in many ways as a moral center of the University regarding issues of equity and fairness.
The curriculum provided by AAF is a mainstay of cultural, social and historical understanding and a critical and defining part of the American narrative, a narrative that is wholly American, not just singularly Black American.

Recent articulation of the transformational goals and mission of the University directly spell out the necessary movement from institutionalized racism to new constructs of diversity (racial and ethnic affirmation for all people) and inclusion.
The proposal for departmental status is not a reactionary idea.
The expectations and goals of AAF have come to far exceed ‘program’ status.
It is critical that AAF be confirmed as a department because AAF needs the designation to create the infrastructure to develop its relevance to our students and build our curriculum.
Departmental status will situate AAF in a more competitive position to attract internal and external funding recruit new faculty, recruit students to the major and minor, and enlarge our capacity to respond nationally and globally, in more informed ways, to an increasing demand for justice.

2 Gender and Women’s Studies Program: See Appendix B To make Gender and Women’s Studies an academic department rather than a program. In designating Gender and Women’s Studies (GWS) as a “Department,” URI will affirm that GWS is equal in status and importance to all other Departments at URI. Consistent with the goals outlined in the Academic Strategic Plan (2016-2021), this change will demonstrate unequivocally URI’s commitment to student success, diversity, and social justice—all at the core of GWS teaching and scholarship. Except for being accorded equal status as a “Department,” since 1972, GWS has operated just like other departments. GWS has its own budget, “director” who participates in all chair obligations and duties, growing number of majors (45 in FY2021) and minors, TT, full-time, and joint faculty lines, an endowed chair, URI Foundation funds, student scholarships, sponsored events, and a graduate certificate program that has graduated over 30 students. But it is time now to give GWS equal status.

RATIONALE: There should be a demonstrable purpose and documented need for the proposed organizational change. 1.
Explain why the organizational change is being proposed.
Africana Studies has been a program at the University of Rhode Island for more than three decades.
During that time, Africana Studies (referred to as AAF) has always embodied the values of racial and social justice.
AAF has served in many ways as a moral center of the University regarding issues of equity and fairness.
The curriculum provided by AAF is a mainstay of cultural, social and historical understanding and a critical and defining part of the American narrative, a narrative that is wholly American, not just singularly Black American.
Recent articulation of the transformational goals and mission of the University directly spell out the necess ary movement from institutionalized racism to new constructs of diversity (racial and ethnic affirmation for all people) and inclusion.

Given the recent events of George Floyd's tragic death and other killings of Black men and women at the hands of American police officers, our nation is embroiled in a resurgence of racial conflict.
The urgency of this time in history is to re -think our commitments to racial equity.
It is a time for our institution to review policies and practices and confront long-standing institutional racism.
Specifically, URI has begun to respond to these exigencies by confronting the issues of institutional racism through enacting courses of action that are direct and measurable.
As part of that important response, we propose the explicit endorsement of Africana Studies to departmental status.
The proposal for departmental status is not a reactionary idea.
The expectations and goals of AAF have come to far exceed 'program' status.
It is critical that AAF be confirmed as a department because AAF needs the designation to create the infrastructure to develop its relevance to our students and build our curriculum.

Departmental status will situate AAF in a more competitive position to attract internal and external funding recruit new faculty, recruit students to the major and minor, and enlarge our capacity to respond nationally and globally, in more informed ways, to an increasing demand for justice.
As the state's flagship public research institution, the University of Rhode Island is a vibrant and dynamic community that is connected by: a common quest for knowledge to transform the way we perceive and understand the world; a sincere desire for innovation to enrich the campus community and the state of Rhode Island; and a real commitment to embrace social justice and to promote civic engage-ment.
These same connecting principles (i.e., knowledge, innovation, social justice, civic engagement, etc.) are the foundations upon which the Department of Africana Studies were established, over thirty years ago.

More importantly, these same principles have guided the Department in its efforts to coordinate and collaborate, with other public institutions of higher education (i.e., Rhode Island College, the Community College of Rhode Island, etc.), while ensuring an environment designed to enhance college teaching, learning, research, and student development.
Since the inception of Africana Studies, at the University of Rhode Island, affiliated faculty have been consistently recognized as established leaders in their respected academic fields (i.e., African American History and culture, Art and Art History, English and Film Media, Philosophy and African American Literature, Communication Studies, Clinical Psychology, Environmental Sciences, Religion Studies, Sociology, etc.), and have also been acknowledged for providing undergraduate, graduate, and professional students with the

3 distinctive educational opportunities expected of a major research university, especially opportunities to negotiate the trans-disciplinary nature of Africana Studies.
In recent years the University of Rhode Island has recognized the teaching, research, and scholarship that defines Africana Studies, and the critically important role our faculty has played in preparing a new generation of students, not only with the analytical and theoretical skills necessary to understand the intersections of racial difference and inequality, but with the cultural competencies necessary to provide transformational leadership in every aspect of American society.
Consequently, we sincerely hope that this request for organizational change will enable the university to appoint tenured/tenured -track faculty, in Africana Studies, consistent with other flagship public research universities throughout New England and around the country, including the University of Connecticut, the University of Massachusetts Amherst, Buffalo State: The State University of New York, and The Pennsylvania State University.

AAF for many years has been treated like a department in the College in the Arts and Sciences with the Director attending all Chair meetings, operating budget allocated, PTF funding allocated and event funding allocated.
Thus, the change to department status will recognize the current status and operations of the AAF program within the College of Arts and Sciences.
In other words, AAF is already functioning like a department and this organizational change will visibly demonstrate this for the campus and for the prospective students and faculty.
More importantly, a more strongly supported and validated Africana Studies Department will help URI students to prepare to face and engage in national and global communities successfully.
Africana Studies can help meet this need not just for Students of Color, but for all students.
Africana Studies affirmed as a Department can also help lead the way for URI to address institutional racism within our own University and the Rhode Island and New England region.

Because of the nation-wide systemic neglect of Africana programs, taking this initiative positions URI to lead other universities throughout the nation in correcting a lack of institutional support for their Africana Studies programs/ departments.
With departmental status, Africana Studies is poised to contribute to African research.
First, several of our faculty are internationally recognized scholars in the area of African research.
Secondly, URI has developed on-going research relationships through the Biological Sciences and Marine Affairs Departments and both departments have invited Africana Studies to participate in several research projects.
For instance, we are currently working as a consultant with Dr.
Brian Crawford and the US Aid Fisheries Program to establish Covid-19 public health initiatives in the Cape Coast, Ghana area.
In addition, Africana Studies has developed relationships with the Faculty of The University of Ghana at Accra and The University of Cape Coast, Cape Coast, Ghana.
Thirdly, URI through Africana Studies has developed successful Study Abroad programs in Ghana and nearby Cape Verde.

Africana Studies outreach has taken us to Bermuda, Trinidad and Tobago and we have received invitations to Jamaica and St.
Lucia to explore connections between West Indian cultures, the Caribbean and African Americans.
The opportunities for growth and expansion are plentiful but the ability to attract funding, internal and external grants are stymied by the program status.
Departmental status for Africana Studies would increase URI's visibility and respectability in the scholarly communities within the African Diaspora.
The proposed change of status, from program to department, would be a demonstrable stride toward directly confronting institutional racism at URI.
Initiatives toward diversity have not been strong enough to deinstitutionalize long-standing apathy toward Africana Studies.
Departmental status would be a measurable, clear and strong expression of anti-racism, a proactive dismantling of institutionalized racism and classicism.

INSTITUTIONAL ROLE: The organizational change should be clearly related to the published role and mission of the institution and be compatible with the organizational structure of the institution 1. Explain how the organizational change is consistent with published role and mission of institution and how it is related to institutional planning The organizational change of Africana Studies from program to departmental status would be consistent with the published role and mission of URI, specifically as it relates to institutional planning of goals and initiatives for transformational change (diversity, equity and inclusion). As the discipline that focuses primarily on the African and African American presence in the world, Africana Studies is uniquely in sync with the goals for transformational change. Africana Studies as a department could better fulfill the initiatives of The Community, Equity & Diversity Strategic Plan 2017 - 2022 as well as those outlined by Dean Jen Riley, College of Arts & Sciences in her letter of June 11, 2020. Africana Studies will be better positioned as a department to enact the following goals, strategies and actions. Goal #1 of CED Strategic Plan, Recruitment • Encourage undergraduate students from marginalized groups to apply for graduate school at URI. This will provide a valuable service to undergraduate students, with a secondary benefit to URI graduate recruitment. Departmental status will enable Africana Studies to interface with more undergraduate students from marginalized groups and walk with them more comprehensively through graduate school preparation.

5 • Work with academic units to identify and expand URI's connections with minority-serving institutions (e.g., Asian American and Pacific Islander institutions, historically black colleges and universities, Hispanic-serving institutions, tribal colleges and universities, and women's colleges) to expand URI's network of diverse applicants.
Africana Studies is one such academic unit that can clearly identify and expand URI's connections with institutions that serve Students of Color and marginalized students.
Specifically, Africana Studies interacts with historically Black colleges, Hispanic-serving institutions and Colleges that serve Native American students.
For example, Africana Studies is a major sponsor and host in support of the URI DIVE Student Conference that welcomes Students of Color from all over the New England region; Africana Studies works closely with the Narragansett Native American community in our own state of Rhode Island.
Africana Studies sponsors URI Students of Color as they attend Conferences and special events at historically Black colleges.

We are currently working to create a Black Student Support Consortium between Black students at historically Black Colleges and State Universities such as URI.
Departmental status for Africana Status will enable us to do this kind of outreach more effectively and strengthen our ability to expand URI's network of diverse applicants.
Goal #2 of CED Strategic Plan, Retention • Offer discussion lunches for all faculty; strongly encourage faculty members from marginalized groups, along with their mentors, to attend.
Departmental status will enable Africana Studies to be substantively encouraging of Faculty of Color and proactively organized in developing mentoring opportunities for Faculty of Color.
Africana Studies fully supports Discussion lunches and would strongly encourage Faculty of Color to attend (along with their mentors).
Department status will also bring more recognition to service contributions and collaborations by faculty in the annual review process. • Acknowledge and publicize accomplishments, contributions, and career milestones for employees.

Affirming innovation in research, teaching, and service of faculty from marginalized groups is a way to convey the many ways in which people from marginalized groups contribute to the community.
For too long the university has been negligent in recognizing Faculty of Color.
Africana Studies needs Departmental status to be effective in advocating for the recognition of Faculty of Color at the Departmental and University levels.
As noted previously, departmental status can also assist with recruiting new faculty to URI.
Finally, Africana Studies is uniquely aligned to deliver Strategy 3 of the CED Strategic Plan, to address the mental models and assumptions that reflect unconscious bias, taken-for-granted beliefs, perceptions, thoughts, and feelings rooted in the oppression of community members from marginalized groups.
With the affirmation of Departmental Status, Africana Studies can lead the way in modeling, providing guidance, and encouraging equity-mindedness in planning and decision- making processes across the institution.

A Department of Africana Studies can also work with the Office of the Provost and with the Faculty Senate to encourage diversity expectations in the tenure review process and to broaden criteria for research, teaching, and service. 2.

RATIONALE: There should be a demonstrable purpose and documented need for the proposed organizational change.
Rationale for becoming the Department of Gender and Women's Studies instead of the Gender and Women's Studies Program Overview: In designating Gender and Women's Studies (GWS) as a "Department," URI will affirm that GWS is equal in status and importance to all other Departments at URI.
Consistent with the goals outlined in the Academic Strategic Plan (2016-2021), this change will demonstrate unequivocally URI's commitment to student success, diversity, and social justice-all at the core of GWS teaching and scholarship.
Except for being accorded equal status as a "Department," since 1972, GWS has operated just like other departments.

GWS has its own budget, "director" who participates in all chair obligations and duties, growing number of majors (45 in FY2021) and minors, TT, full-time, and joint faculty lines, an endowed chair, URI Foundation funds, student scholarships, sponsored events, and a graduate certificate program that has graduated over 30 students.
But it is time now to give GWS equal status.
The current and pressing historical issues in our society-#MeToo, #BlackLivesMatter, the 2020 Centennial of the Women's Vote, and the struggle for LGBTQ rights-make it clear that leaders must take action to create equality in their institutions.
This organization change can and will make URI a leader among its peers.
This proposed change to "Department" will be a visible declaration at URI of the equal stature it accords all of its academic units.
Insofar as human rights, equality, and anti- racism teaching and scholarship are also integral to the discipline of Gender and Women's Studies, this proposed change will recognize the crucial work GWS does at URI.
Currently, there are more than 800 GWS departments nationally, but none in RI.

As the flagship university, URI will lead in establishing the first GWS department in RI, placing URI in the good company of "aspiring to be like" institutions, the University of Delaware https://www.wgs.udel.edu/academics/wgs and the University of Virginia https://wgs.as.virginia.edu/.
Specific Outcomes and rationales: As a "Department," Gender and Women's Studies will be one among equals in the College of Arts & Sciences and at URI, and across the professions, generating the following outcomes: • Affirm the value and place of Gender and Women's Studies in a university that seeks to uphold the values of diversity, equality, antiracism, and social justice.
GWS as a discipline focuses on the teaching of human rights, LGBTQ rights, social justice, Black Lives Matter, and the Me Too Movement.
The intersectional approach central to the discipline of GWS demands and enacts the study of simultaneous oppressions related to race, class, gender, sexuality, ageism, disabilities.
This intersectional approach and pedagogy positions GWS as central to educating students to understand and 2

3 address current and future national and global historical and political crises.
GWS at URI and in the world is a leader in antiracist teaching.
The designation as Department will recognize and validate GWS's role in impacting the antiracist intellectual and cultural climate and practices at the university and beyond. • Validate and honor the interdisciplinary discipline of GWS in its own right.
URI's Academic Plan places high value on interdisciplinary work.
Gender and Women's Studies is a formal interdisciplinary field unto itself.
Scholarly journals: GWS has about 40 journals worldwide dedicated to its scholarship.
A scan of the list at the end of the Rationale reveals the vast number of interdisciplinary foci that are all considered part of GWS.
Two of the journals coming out of URI are not on the Internet search list but should be: Dignity and Journal of Feminist Scholarship.
Associations and Conferences: GWS has hundreds of gender conferences and organizations worldwide, including the National Women's Studies Association, a global organization founded in 1977 with membership in the thousands and an annual conference attended by thousands.

NWSA's stated goals speak to the interdisciplinary nature inherent to the field of Gender and Women's Studies: "to demonstrate the contributions of feminist scholarship that is comparative, global, intersectional and interdisciplinary to understandings of the arts, humanities, social sciences and sciences; and to promote synergistic relationships between scholarship, teaching and civic engagement in understandings of culture and society." Leadership in the world: UN Women, established in 2010 as a major global working group, also articulates the many disciplines and subjects that come together in GWS: Leadership and political participation; economic empowerment; ending violence against women; peace and security; humanitarian action; youth; governance and national planning; sustainable development; HIV and AIDs.

While UN Women "focuses on priority areas that are fundamental to women's equality," they also recognize that this equality "unlock[s] progress across the board." As UN Women states: "All human development and human rights issues have gender dimensions." URI is long overdue in recognizing both the rightful position and place of interdisciplinary disciplines as valid and complete in themselves, and the rightful and important role GWS plays in educating students, faculty, staff, and the world on the many ways gender matters.
On the one hand, the creation of an academic department formalizes the role and responsibility of the Chair, faculty, and affiliated faculty, institutionally strengthening the academic major and course of study.
On the other hand, designating GWS as a department validates the interdisciplinary validity of this field in its own right. • Lend more credibility for students looking to major or double major in GWS.
Students will understand their investment in GWS as a single or double major as equally validating as majoring in all other departments.

In addition, on a transcript, majoring in a "Department" rather than a "Program" may also be perceived by employers and graduate programs as more substantial and equal to majors in other "Departments." As a department, with equal recognition and validation as all other departments, socially justice-minded prospective students and young scholars whose work, teaching, and passion are grounded in gender, equal rights, and social justice work will be all the more drawn to courses and majoring or double majoring in GWS. • Enhance the connections between many URI departments and faculty involved in the study of gender, equality, and social justice.
Department designation will encourage more administrators, faculty, and students to affiliate and collaborate with GWS.
Research indicates that where an organization has status differentials, including between a "Department"' and a "Program," cross- pollination and collaboration are less likely to occur.
As the GWS Department, other departments and administrators will be inclined to take GWS more seriously and reach out more to GWS as equal stakeholders.

4 • Bring URI in line with colleges and universities around the country, including universities URI aspires to and competes with for students and faculty.
There are approximately 800 universities around the country that have acquired Department status and others, like us, are seeking it.
In RI, no other college or university currently has department designation for their GWS programs.
As a Flagship University, URI should be at least up to par with our peer or "aspiring-to-be-like" institutions. "Thinking Big," URI should strive to be a leader in education and organizational design.
In RI, especially, URI should be the first to accomplish this important goal. • Attract highly competitive and diverse faculty who wish to be part of a fully recognized "Department" rather than "Program." In promotion and tenure decisions, it is also possible that working for a "Department" will be seen as more valuable, permanent, and reputable than working for a "Program." • Create growing interest in GWS leadership.
As a Department with a "Chair" instead of a "Director," faculty might be more interested in taking on the position as "Chair" of Gender and Women's Studies. • Attract external funding.

As a Department, getting grants for an individual or a department as a whole may have more credibility than getting grants for a "Program." To external funders and reviewers, programs may appear more ad hoc and less permanent than departments.
Those seeking to support research and scholarship are likely to seek more permanent "homes" for resource allocation. • Send a powerful message to all URI alumni and to GWS alumni conveying URI's commitment to the value, teaching, and scholarship of gender and women's studies, including a focus on: LGBTQ rights, black lives matter, the Me Too Movement, and global human rights.
Showing alumni the unequivocal support for a Department of GWS will perhaps catalyze more gift giving, scholarships, and further endowments. • Send a powerful message of support to URI students, faculty, and staff who are women, LGBTQ, nonbinary, and males advocating for equal rights URI's commitment to the value, teaching, and scholarship of gender and women's issues.

Our transformative curriculum comes alive through our students, their actions, and their success at URI and beyond.
GWS gives URI students the education and skills to thrive and lead in a multicultural, diverse, antiracist world and workplace.
Foundational to the GWS program is praxis: theory and action.
We transmit to our students the know-how and skills to create the world they want to live in through timely coursework that includes engaged learning opportunities here and abroad.
